strengths: The paper identifies a genuine and well-articulated limitation of existing feed-forward 3DGS models—the coupling of representation density to input image resolution and the quadratic cost of full multi-view attention—and proposes concrete architectural solutions (decoupled viewpoint embeddings, two-stage cross/self-attention, token uplifting) that address both problems.

The decoupling of Gaussian generation from pixel-aligned input views is a conceptually clean and useful contribution: it enables compact 3D representations that are independent of input resolution, and the ablation in Table 8 ('w/o resolution decoupling') and Table 12 (different viewpoint resolutions) provide direct evidence for its benefit.

Empirical results are strong and broad. iLRM achieves state-of-the-art PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS on RE10K (Table 1), outperforms MVSplat/DepthSplat on cross-dataset ACID and DL3DV (Table 2), beats DepthSplat on DL3DV across view configurations (Table 3), and beats optimization-based 3D-GS/Mip-splatting and LongLRM in the wide-coverage setting (Table 5), all while substantially reducing inference time and memory (e.g., 0.025s vs 0.065s/0.114s and 1.40GB vs 3.55GB).

The paper is well-organized and readable, with clear motivation, a coherent method section, and a thorough ablation suite covering model depth, attention design, initialization, resolution decoupling, and token uplifting (Tables 6-9, 10-12).

Reproducibility is good: the supplementary provides detailed hyperparameters, training schedules, Gaussian parameterization, camera-pose normalization, FLOP calculations, and additional qualitative/quantitative results.
The theoretical FLOP analysis (Section F) and the structural comparison in Fig. 2 give a useful, principled justification for the scalability claims rather than relying only on wall-clock numbers.
weaknesses: The central 'iterative refinement' framing is somewhat oversold. In practice the model is a stack of transformer layers whose viewpoint tokens are updated by cross- and self-attention; there is no explicit rendering-error feedback or gradient-like signal from a rendered estimate as in per-scene optimization. The analogy to optimization-based 3D-GS is a useful narrative device but the mechanism is standard layer-wise representation refinement, and the intermediate-layer visualizations in Fig. 1 (Layers #6/#8/#10) could be misleading since only the final layer's tokens are decoded into Gaussians.

The mini-batch cross-attention variants (MC) trade quality for speed in a way that partly undercuts the efficiency story: e.g., at 8 views PSNR drops from 31.57 to 30.96 and at 4 views from 30.37 to 30.10 (Table 1), while the accuracy drop is attributed to sampling rather than to any principled reason the subsampling is unbiased. The claims of 'improving scalability without sacrificing performance' are not fully supported by these numbers.

The method requires known camera poses, which is acknowledged as a limitation but is increasingly restrictive relative to pose-free and single-image feed-forward methods; the practical value would be strengthened by at least a robustness experiment to pose noise.

Comparison breadth is somewhat uneven: GS-LRM is marked as having no official code/pretrained models (Table 1), and iterative-refinement competitors G3R and Gen-Den are only compared in Table 1/2 without the depth of analysis applied to MVSplat/DepthSplat. It is hard to fully gauge the marginal gain over the closest iterative-refinement prior work.

Some architectural choices (e.g., expansion factor k=2 for token uplifting, use of separate parameters per update block, the specific structured mini-batch schemes) are empirically set without much justification or sensitivity analysis, leaving open how sensitive the reported gains are to these hyperparameters.

The self-attention across viewpoints remains the scalability bottleneck and the paper acknowledges this, but the experiments only go up to 32 views; the scaling claims would be more convincing with a broader view-count sweep (e.g., 50-100 views) to demonstrate where the method actually breaks down.

strengths: The paper targets a well-identified and practically important bottleneck in feed-forward 3D Gaussian reconstruction: pixel-aligned Gaussian generation scales with input image resolution, and full attention over all multi-view image tokens grows quadratically in both view count and resolution. The motivation is clearly articulated and supported by concrete examples (e.g., 200M Gaussians for a 200-view scene versus ~0.5M needed).

The architecture is clean and thoughtfully designed: viewpoint-centric embeddings decoupled from input images, per-view cross-attention followed by self-attention over the compact viewpoint token set, token up-lifting to bridge the LR-viewpoint/HR-image resolution mismatch, and structured mini-batch cross-attention. Figure 2 provides a concrete relative-compute analysis (1:1:0.25:0.08), which makes the scalability claim tangible rather than rhetorical.

The iterative-refinement formulation (each layer = one 'optimization step' consuming image features as gradient-like signals) is a sensible way to import the strengths of per-scene optimization into a feed-forward model, and the ablation in Table 8 (w/o iterative refinement: 29.24 -> 28.58 PSNR) provides direct evidence that it matters.

Experimental breadth is good: RE10K, DL3DV and ACID, several viewpoint/resolution configurations, comparisons against pixelSplat, MVSplat, GS-LRM, DepthSplat and Gen-Den, plus optimization-based 3D-GS, Mip-splatting and LongLRM in the wide-coverage setting. The fair 2-view full-resolution setting (2, F, F) still improves over baselines at the same 131k Gaussian budget and with lower inference time, so the gains are not solely attributable to extra input views.

Ablations are reasonably comprehensive and isolate the contribution of each component: number of update layers, iterative refinement, resolution decoupling, token up-lifting, mini-batch cross-attention variants, self-attention vs. group attention, and representation initialization. Efficiency ablations (Table 6, Table 11) show substantial FLOP/memory reductions with small quality drops.

The supplementary material is unusually detailed on implementation (Gaussian parameter decoding, camera pose normalization, training schedule, tokenization and normalization), which materially improves reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental. The three central ingredients - decoupling the scene representation from input images via learned viewpoint embeddings (as in LRM/LaRa/QuArk-style representations), iterative refinement that mimics optimization (as in G3R/Gen-Den), and cross-then-self alternating attention over a compact token set (as in VGGT) - are each individually established. The contribution is a well-executed combination plus a practical mini-batch attention scheme, but the conceptual advance over prior work is limited, and the 'first implementation' framing overstates the novelty.

The headline comparisons in Table 1 are not fully apples-to-apples. The best rows (Ours (4, H, F) = 29.24, Ours (8, H, F) = 30.39) use 4 and 8 input views while pixelSplat, MVSplat, GS-LRM and DepthSplat use the standard 2-view RE10K protocol in the same table. No baseline is evaluated at a matched number of input views on RE10K, so part of the reported margin reflects additional input information rather than the architecture alone. This should be separated explicitly (e.g., a matched-view baseline row), even though the (2, F, F) row does provide a fair comparison.

There is a text-to-table inconsistency regarding training cost: Section 3.5 states 'We report detailed comparisons of computational costs during training in Tab. 6', but Table 6 contains only the authors' own mini-batch cross-attention variants with no baseline training cost (iteration time, memory). The training-efficiency claim relative to prior work is therefore not directly substantiated, only FLOPs for the authors' own variants are given.

Sensitivity to camera pose quality is acknowledged only as a limitation. Given that the method relies on accurate poses and that the viewpoint tokenization is built from Plücker ray embeddings, an experiment quantifying degradation under pose noise (or with poses from COLMAP/SfM rather than dataset ground truth) would substantially strengthen the practical claims. No such experiment is presented.

Several design choices are set empirically without sensitivity analysis or justification, notably the token up-lifting expansion factor k = 2 and the patch size p = 8; it is unclear how sensitive the efficiency/quality trade-off is to these values, and whether the reported gains persist at other operating points.

The comparison against LongLRM in Table 5 relies on differently-tuned variants (LongLRM_10 and Ours_10/Ours_50 with differing finetuning schedules, A100 vs. H100 hardware), which makes the speed and quality conclusions harder to attribute to the method rather than to the finetuning budget. Similarly, GS-LRM is only cited from reported numbers because code/checkpoints are unavailable, which the authors correctly flag but which still weakens the strongest quality comparison.

strengths: The problem is well motivated and clearly presented: the quadratic cost of full attention over multi-view image tokens in feed-forward 3DGS models is a real and important scalability bottleneck, and the paper articulates this crisply in the introduction.

The core design idea—decoupling a low-resolution, image-independent set of viewpoint tokens from high-resolution image tokens, so that Gaussians are generated compactly while still being guided by HR visual features—is sensible and practically useful. The resulting representations are indeed much more compact (e.g., ~172k Gaussians vs. 688k for DepthSplat at comparable quality in Tab. 3).

The empirical evaluation is broad: RE10K, DL3DV, ACID, cross-dataset generalization, wide-coverage settings, and a substantial set of ablations (model size in Tab. 7, architecture variants in Tabs. 8/9, mini-batch attention in Tab. 6, view-overlap in Tab. 10, equal-Gaussian-count in Tab. 11, viewpoint resolution in Tab. 12).

The efficiency results are concrete and non-trivial: consistent reductions in inference time, memory, and Gaussian count relative to MVSplat/DepthSplat, with what appear to be competitive rendering metrics.
The qualitative comparisons (Figs. 5–7, 9–11) look strong and are consistent with the quantitative tables.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental. Each ingredient—Plücker-ray viewpoint tokenization, alternating per-view cross-attention plus global self-attention, token upsampling/query expansion, and structured mini-batch attention—has close precedents (VGGT's alternating attention, Quark's embedding-based multi-view fusion, GS-LRM's pose normalization and decoding, G3R/Gen-Den's iterative refinement). The paper itself acknowledges the VGGT connection, so the contribution is largely a recombination plus engineering.

The central 'iterative refinement' claim is overstated. The model does not implement a feedback loop that renders the current estimate, measures error, and updates—it simply stacks cross-attention layers with image features injected at each layer. This is deep transformer stacking dressed as an optimization analogy. Worse, the ablation intended to validate it (Tab. 8, 'w/o iter. refinement') actually removes image-feature injection, not the iterative mechanism, so the paper's headline claim is not cleanly tested.

Missing comparisons to the most relevant recent work. G3R and Gen-Den (iterative refinement) and Quark/VGGT-style embedding models are discussed at length in the related-work section but never compared quantitatively, despite being the closest points of reference. The claim that iLRM 'outperforms existing methods' is therefore only supported against a subset of baselines.

Comparison fairness is questionable. The strongest tabulated baselines are far smaller in parameter count (MVSplat 12M, pixelSplat 125M) than iLRM (171M+), so the reported PSNR gaps (e.g., 28.65 vs. 25.89 in Tab. 1) conflate architecture with capacity. GS-LRM is marked '*' (no code/pretrained model available) and its numbers appear copied from the original paper under a possibly different protocol, undermining the speed and quality comparison.

No variance, seed, or significance reporting. Several conclusions rest on small deltas (e.g., 29.01 vs. 29.24 PSNR between 9 and 12 layers in Tab. 7; the mini-batch cross-attention drop of 30.39→30.25 in Tab. 6), which cannot be judged as meaningful without statistics.

Some quantitative claims are imprecise. The '0.5 seconds for inference' claim only applies to the 32-view wide-coverage setting (Tab. 5 reports 0.19 s for 16 views), and the paper does not always make the per-setting caveats explicit in the abstract-level claims.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code release is evident in the manuscript, and several training details (curriculum, finetuning schedules, memory comparison setups with gradient checkpointing on/off) are relegated to supplementary material.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuine and well-articulated limitation of existing feed-forward 3DGS models—pixel-aligned Gaussians couple representation density to input image resolution, producing redundant Gaussians and quadratic attention cost—and proposes a coherent architectural remedy: decoupling viewpoint-centric tokens from image tokens and iteratively refining them.

The iterative refinement formulation with feedback-driven cross-attention at every layer is conceptually appealing and is supported by the attention visualization (Fig. 8, Fig. 18), which shows that attended tokens progressively converge to geometrically/semantically corresponding regions across layers. This provides interpretable evidence for the design motivation.

Empirical evidence is broad and reasonably strong: evaluation on RE10K, DL3DV, ACID, Tanks&Temples, and Mip-NeRF360, with ablations on model size, architecture (iterative refinement, resolution decoupling, token uplifting), mini-batch cross-attention, viewpoint resolution, and robustness to camera pose perturbations.

Efficiency claims are concretely supported. The method produces far fewer Gaussians (e.g., 172K vs 688K–2.7M for DepthSplat) while achieving better quality, and inference (0.5s) is orders of magnitude faster than per-scene optimization (~8 min) and competitive with or faster than Long-LRM, including at large view counts where Long-LRM runs out of memory (Tab. 15).

The mini-batch (quarter) cross-attention design is validated quantitatively (Tab. 8: 3.83 → 0.81 GFLOPs with only a small PSNR drop), and the theoretical FLOP/attention-cost analysis (Fig. 2) is clearly presented.
The controlled comparison under the same number of Gaussians (Tab. 17) is a fair and informative experiment that isolates the benefit of resolution decoupling from raw representation capacity.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the core ingredients—perceiver-style per-view cross-attention, viewpoint token refinement, alternating cross/self-attention, and mini-batch token sampling—are largely recombinations of existing ideas (e.g., LRM/VGGT-style alternating attention, G3R/Gen-Den iterative refinement, Perceiver sampling). The specific combination is useful but the individual components are not new.

The 'interpretation' of the update as gradient-descent-like (V^(l) ≈ V^(l-1) - η∇_V E) is a loose metaphor rather than a formal result; no gradient is actually computed and no theoretical guarantee or formal equivalence is established. Presenting it in this framing overstates the conceptual depth.

Gains are marginal in several key settings (e.g., DL3DV 32-view: 24.30 vs Long-LRM 23.97 PSNR), and the headline advantage often comes bundled with efficiency rather than quality alone. On some benchmarks the improvement is within noise, so the strongest claim is scalability/efficiency rather than accuracy.

The representation is essentially fixed-size (Gaussian count determined by viewpoint resolution), which decouples from scene complexity; the paper does not explore adaptive/density-aware allocation, so a genuinely complex scene may be under-represented while simple scenes waste capacity.

Several comparisons are confounded by differing training budgets (8×H100, 200K iterations for some configs; different batch sizes; some baselines retrained). Although Tab. 17 partly addresses this, the fairness of the headline quality comparisons is not fully established.
No comparison against more recent strong baselines such as VGGT or other 2024–2025 generalizable reconstruction models beyond Long-LRM/MVSplat/DepthSplat, which weakens the claim of state-of-the-art.

The limitations section is brief and does not discuss failure modes (e.g., reflective/transparent surfaces, large unbounded scenes), and the reliance on accurate camera poses and static scenes is acknowledged but not quantified beyond a simple pose-noise ablation.

Theoretical FLOP analysis (Fig. 2, Sec. E) ignores constant factors, token uplifting overhead, and memory-bandwidth effects; measured speedups (Tab. 8) diverge from the idealized ratios, so the complexity argument is only partially corroborated.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated architectural idea: decoupling the 3D Gaussian representation (viewpoint embeddings) from the input images allows the model to use compact low-resolution scene tokens while still leveraging high-resolution image features as visual evidence, which directly addresses the quadratic scaling problem of prior feed-forward models (GS-LRM, MVSplat, DepthSplat).

Strong and comprehensive empirical validation: results are reported on RE10K, DL3DV, ACID (cross-dataset), Tanks&Temples, and Mip-NeRF360, with the proposed method achieving the best PSNR among open methods on RE10K (28.65) and large gains on cross-dataset DL3DV (25.35 vs 22.92 for DepthSplat) and ACID (29.24 vs 28.61).

Convincing efficiency/scalability story: inference in ~0.03-0.5s with memory of 1.2-3.5 GB versus 3.55-5.87 GB for baselines, and demonstrated scaling to 256 input views without OOM, where Long-LRM runs out of memory.

Thorough ablation study covering model depth (Table 6), architectural components (Table 7), cross-attention mini-batch schemes (Table 8), initialization strategies, and self-attention vs group attention (Table 9), which substantiates the design choices.

Useful supplementary material: depth estimation, geometry (Chamfer/F-score) evaluation, camera-pose robustness, inference-time scaling, and attention visualizations (Fig. 8/18) that support the claimed progressive refinement behavior.

The two-stage (per-view cross-attention + global self-attention) factorization and the mini-batch cross-attention scheme are simple, practical, and yield concrete computational savings (0.81 vs 3.83 GFLOPs) with negligible quality loss.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the core mechanism (iteratively updating latent scene tokens via per-layer cross-attention with image tokens followed by self-attention) is closely related to Perceiver-style iterative-attention architectures. The claimed analogy to gradient-descent optimization is an interpretive framing rather than a formally derived algorithm, so the conceptual contribution is largely an effective architectural recombination.

The mini-batch ('quarter') cross-attention uses structured token subsampling rather than the theoretically preferable random sampling; this is an implementation-driven heuristic and the paper does not deeply analyze how the subsampling pattern affects final reconstruction fidelity.

The method relies on accurate camera poses (Plücker ray embeddings); the limitations section acknowledges this, but no pose-free or joint pose-refinement variant is actually evaluated, leaving a significant practical constraint unaddressed.

Some headline comparisons are marginal: on the 32-view DL3DV setting, the method (24.30 PSNR / 0.803 SSIM) is slightly below optimization-based 3D-GS (24.43 / 0.827), and the strongest baseline on RE10K (GS-LRM, 28.10) is closed-source, so the 'outperforms existing methods' claim is partly restricted to open baselines.

Geometry accuracy is assessed only indirectly via a monocular pseudo-depth estimator (MoGe-2) and pseudo-ground-truth pointmaps, rather than true ground-truth geometry, which weakens the evidence for the geometric-fidelity claims.

The compactness advantage (fewer Gaussians, e.g., 172k vs 688k) is presented as a strength, but the controlled same-Gaussian-count comparison (Table 17) is limited to a small subset, so it is not fully disentangled whether gains come from the architecture or from output-density differences.

strengths: Tackles a genuine and important scalability bottleneck in feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting: the quadratic cost of full attention over (number of views) x (image resolution). The motivation and problem framing are clear and well-grounded.

The decoupling of viewpoint tokens from input image tokens is a clean, practical design. It yields compact, controllable Gaussian sets (e.g., Table 3: 172k Gaussians vs DepthSplat's 688k) and removes the tight coupling between input resolution and representation density, which is a real limitation of pixel-aligned methods.

The empirical evaluation is broad and multi-dataset (RE10K, DL3DV, ACID, Tanks&Temples, Mip-NeRF360), covering cross-dataset generalization, varying view counts/resolutions, wide-baseline and wide-coverage settings, plus depth/geometry proxies and robustness to pose noise.

Efficiency results are substantial and well documented: lower memory (Tables 3, 17), faster inference (Tables 5, 10, 15), and the ability to scale to 256 views where Long-LRM runs out of memory (Table 15). These are concrete, useful gains.

Ablations (Tables 6-9, 18) give reasonable support for the roles of resolution decoupling, token uplifting, self-attention, and number of update layers, and the attention visualizations (Figs. 8, 18) provide qualitative insight into progressive refinement.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty. The headline 'iterative refinement' is essentially standard layer-wise transformer stacking; the footnote concedes it is 'repeatedly updated layer by layer under static (unchanged) image evidence.' Decoupled query tokens, cross-then-self attention, and token upsampling are all established (Perceiver, LRM, Quark), so the paper is largely a well-engineered combination of known techniques rather than a new mechanism.

The 'feedback-driven' and gradient-descent analogy (interpretation around Eq. 3) is post-hoc and superficial: the image evidence S is static, so there is no actual feedback loop. Presenting V^(l) ~ V^(l-1) - eta*grad E as resembling optimization overstates the conceptual contribution.

The ablation intended to justify iterative refinement (Table 7) is not diagnostic: it replaces per-layer cross-attention with a single cross-attention, conflating 'iterative refinement' with merely 'having cross-attention in every layer.' This does not isolate the claimed mechanism.

The mini-batch/quarter cross-attention mainly reduces training cost; Table 8 shows inference-time differences are negligible. Thus its advertised scalability benefit at inference is limited, and the 'structured sampling inspired by mini-batch gradient descent' is a loose analogy rather than a principled mechanism.

The theoretical FLOPs ratio (1:1:0.25:0.08) substantially overstates practical gains: Table 8 reports only ~1.6x iteration-time reduction (1.51s -> 0.94s), so the efficiency framing is harder to interpret and somewhat inflated.

Comparison fairness/consistency is a concern. Results mix 2/4/8-view and various-resolution configurations with different training budgets (e.g., the best 2-view model is trained 200k iters), and several baselines appear to run at default settings, making it difficult to attribute gains cleanly to the proposed design.

At the 32-view setting (Table 5), optimization-based 3D-GS is better on PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS than the zero-shot model (24.43/0.827/0.191 vs 24.30/0.803/0.256), which the paper does not surface; the broad claim of superior quality needs qualification.

Improvements over the most similar baseline (Long-LRM) are modest (e.g., +0.33 dB PSNR at 32 views), raising the question of whether the added architectural complexity is justified relative to existing scalable models.

The geometry/depth evaluation relies on MoGe-2 pseudo-depth as ground truth (Table 11, Fig. 10), which is circular for assessing geometric fidelity; ground-truth-based metrics (NRGBD, ETH3D) are included but are secondary.
